verses.text: Now a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”
Elisha said to her, “What should I do for you? Tell me: what do you have in the house?” She said, “Your servant has nothing in the house, except a pot of oil.”
Then he said, “Go, borrow empty containers from of all your neighbors. Don’t borrow just a few containers.
Go in and shut the door on you and on your sons, and pour oil into all those containers; and set aside those which are full.”
So she went from him, and shut the door on herself and on her sons. They brought the containers to her, and she poured oil.
When the containers were full, she said to her son, “Bring me another container.” He said to her, “There isn’t another container.” Then the oil stopped flowing.
Then she came and told the man of God. He said, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt; and you and your sons live on the rest.”
One day Elisha went to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread.
She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God who passes by us continually.
Please let us make a little room on the roof. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. When he comes to us, he can stay there.”
One day he came there, and he went to the room and lay there.
He said to Gehazi his servant, “Call this Shunammite.” When he had called her, she stood before him.

He said to him, “Say now to her, ‘Behold, you have cared for us with all this care. What is to be done for you? Would you like to be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the army?’” She answered, “I dwell among my own people.”
He said, “What then is to be done for her?” Gehazi answered, “Most certainly she has no son, and her husband is old.”
He said, “Call her.” When he had called her, she stood in the door.
He said, “At this season, when the time comes around, you will embrace a son.” She said, “No, my lord, you man of God, do not lie to your servant.”
The woman conceived, and bore a son at that season, when the time came around, as Elisha had said to her.
When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers.
He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.”
When he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died.
She went up and laid him on the man of God’s bed, and shut the door on him, and went out.
She called to her husband, and said, “Please send me one of the servants, and one of the donkeys, that I may run to the man of God, and come again.”
He said, “Why would you want go to him today? It is not a new moon or a Sabbath.” She said, “It’s alright.”
Then she saddled a donkey, and said to her servant, “Drive, and go forward! Don’t slow down for me, unless I ask you to.”
So she went, and came to the man of God to Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her afar off, he said to Gehazi his servant, “Behold, there is the Shunammite.
Please run now to meet her, and ask her, ‘Is it well with you? Is it well with your husband? Is it well with your child?’” She answered, “It is well.”

When she came to the man of God to the hill, she caught hold of his feet. Gehazi came near to thrust her away; but the man of God said, “Leave her alone; for her soul is troubled within her; and Yahweh has hidden it from me, and has not told me.”
Then she said, “Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn’t I say, ‘Do not deceive me’?”

Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the child’s face.”
The child’s mother said, “As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So he arose, and followed her.
Gehazi went ahead of them, and laid the staff on the child’s face; but there was no voice and no hearing. Therefore he returned to meet him, and told him, “The child has not awakened.”
When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and lying on his bed.
He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh.
He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the child’s flesh grew warm.
Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself out on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
He called Gehazi, and said, “Call this Shunammite!” So he called her. When she had come in to him, he said, “Take up your son.”
Then she went in, fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground; then she picked up her son, and went out.

Elisha came again to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him; and he said to his servant, “Get the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets.”
One went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered a lap full of wild gourds from it, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew; for they didn’t recognize them.
So they poured out for the men to eat. As they were eating some of the stew, they cried out, and said, “Man of God, there is death in the pot!” And they could not eat it.
But he said, “Then bring meal.” He threw it into the pot; and he said, “Serve it to the people, that they may eat.” And there was nothing harmful in the pot.

A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread some of the first fruits: twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.”
His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for Yahweh says, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’”
So he set it before them, and they ate, and had some left over, according to Yahweh’s word.

footnotes.content: A widow cries out—her husband feared the Lord but left her nothing but debt. She faces losing her sons to slavery, the cruelest poverty of all. Sometimes the faithful fail to provide, and we're left picking up the pieces. The Lord doesn't ignore her cry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha asks first: What do you have? It's a strange question when she has nothing—but she does have one small jar of oil. The Lord often begins with what lies at hand, what seems insignificant. He doesn't demand we find more; He asks us to see what we already hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go borrow empty containers—not a few, but many. This sounds foolish: she has no oil, yet she's to ask neighbors for vessels to fill. Faith sometimes looks like admitting we're about to receive more than we can hold. The neighbors must have wondered, but they lent anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shut the door and pour—privacy for a small miracle. There's something tender about this: she and her sons alone, pouring and watching. The Lord often works in the quiet places, away from witness, between a mother and her children. What happens behind closed doors matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She went and did it. No hesitation, no debate. She brought the vessels and began to pour—and the oil flowed. Obedience isn't waiting to understand everything; it's moving when the man of God speaks, even when the math makes no sense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When she ran out of containers, the oil stopped flowing. There's a boundary, even in abundance—but notice: it stopped only when there was nowhere left to pour. The miracle matched the need, not endless excess. She had exactly what she needed to pay her debts and live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on the rest. Not just rescue, but restoration—she moves from despair to security. This is the Lord's way: He doesn't merely patch a crisis; He gives ground to stand on. She and her sons are no longer slaves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Shunammite woman saw a holy man pass through her town and persuaded him to eat—such a small kindness, yet it opens a door. She had discernment and hospitality without presumption. The best acts of service begin with noticing someone and offering bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She perceived he was a holy man of God. How? Not by his dress or titles, surely, but by something she sensed—his manner, his peace, the way he carried himself. We know the Lord's servants by their fruit, by a certain kindness that speaks of Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A little room on the roof—bed, table, chair, lamp. She didn't offer grandeur, just rest and care. She asked for nothing in return, only the privilege of serving. There's wisdom in knowing exactly what someone needs: a quiet place to lay his head.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He lay in the room she made. He accepted her gift without fanfare or transaction. Sometimes holiness looks like letting others serve you—receiving their care as a blessing to them, not a burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha called her to stand before him. A man of God seeking to bless those who blessed him—he moves from rest to gratitude, wanting to repay kindness. He doesn't let her service pass unnoted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What can I do for you? Offer you a word with the king? She answered: I dwell among my own people. She had no hunger for favor or influence, only contentment in her place. There's a quiet strength in wanting nothing that isn't already yours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi noticed what she lacked: she has no son, and her husband is old. The prophet's servant understood her heart before she spoke it. Sometimes those closest to us see the quiet ache we've learned to live with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He called her to the door. She stood in the threshold, ready to hear. There's something holy about openness—standing where you can hear, willing to receive what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At this season you'll embrace a son—and she recoils: Don't lie to me. Her pain is real enough that she won't let hope deceive her. Yet the Lord speaks a true word anyway, gently holding both her fear and His promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She conceived and bore a son at that season, when Elisha had said. The word came true in exact measure. What the Lord promises through His servant, He fulfills—not as metaphor, but as flesh and breath in her arms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the child was grown, he went out to his father with the reapers—a scene of ordinary joy, a boy running to his father in the field. The miracle is complete; the child lives. But soon this peace will shatter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My head! My head!—sudden, terrible pain. A child's cry, then silence. The father sends him to his mother, not knowing this is death approaching. In one moment, the miracle falls silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sat on her knees until noon, then died. She held her son while life left him. She had carried him once as a promise; now she carries him as loss. The gift returns to the Giver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She laid him on the prophet's bed and shut the door—not in despair yet, but in a quiet act of faith. She placed her dead son on the bed of the man of God, as if to say: He is yours; you spoke him into being; perhaps you can speak him back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Send me a servant and a donkey; I must go to the man of God. She tells no one her son is dead. She just goes—urgency and faith braided together. She will lay this at his feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why go today? It's not a new moon or Sabbath—days when such visits were common. Her husband sees no reason for haste. She just says: It's alright. She knows what he doesn't: her son is dead, and she will not explain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She saddled the donkey herself and told her servant: Don't slow down unless I ask. Urgency and command—she drives forward with the strength of a mother who will not be denied. Drive hard; there is no time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She came to Mount Carmel, the place of Elijah's fire and the Lord's showdown. Elisha saw her from afar and recognized her—the woman who served him, now coming toward him with urgency. The place where prophets meet the Lord's will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is it well with you, your husband, your child? She answered: It is well. Lies are sometimes faith—she will not speak the death aloud until she reaches the prophet. She holds the secret, protecting it until the word of God can meet it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She caught his feet; Gehazi tried to push her away—but Elisha said: Leave her alone; her soul is troubled. The prophet discerns her pain where others see only disorder. He knows the Lord hasn't told him why, yet still he holds space for her grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Did I ask you for a son? Why did you deceive me?—raw accusation, the cry of a mother who believed a word and now holds only a corpse. She names what we all fear: that the Lord gives and takes, and we are left to grieve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take my staff; lay it on the child's face; don't greet anyone—haste and command. Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with no explanation, trusting that obedience will be enough. Sometimes we move toward the impossible without waiting to understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The child's mother said: As the Lord lives, I will not leave you. She will not be separated from the prophet until he comes himself. Her persistence is fierce—not defiance, but the grip of a mother who will not let go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gehazi laid the staff on the child's face, but nothing happened—no voice, no hearing. The staff alone is not enough; the prophet himself must come. Sometimes the servant's obedience must wait for the master's presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The child was dead, lying on Elisha's bed. Death in that room—the place of rest has become a tomb. But the child lies on the prophet's bed, not in the ground. There is a waiting, a hope not yet spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shut the door and prayed to the Lord. Alone with the dead and the Almighty—no witnesses, no performance. This is prayer in its deepest place: a man asking his God to raise the dead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He lay on the child—mouth on mouth, eyes on eyes, hands on hands. The prophet stretched himself over the body, his warmth meeting death. This is incarnation whispered: the living giving life to the dead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walked back and forth, then lay on the child again—and the child sneezed, opened his eyes. Breath returned; life resumed. The sound of a sneeze—so ordinary, yet it marks the boundary between death and restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take up your son—Elisha gave him back to his mother alive. Not merely resurrected, but returned: her child, whole and breathing, restored to her arms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She fell at his feet and bowed to the ground; then picked up her son and went out. Gratitude and restraint braided together—she honors the prophet, then takes her gift and leaves, no words needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha came to Gilgal during famine; the sons of the prophets sat before him. Get the large pot and boil stew—care for those who follow and learn. Even in want, the prophet thinks first of feeding others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One went out and found wild gourds, gathered them into the pot—they didn't recognize them. In hunger, we can mistake danger for food. The appearance of plenty isn't always plenty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As they ate, they cried out: There is death in the pot! They tasted poison before they swallowed it. The Lord sometimes sends bitter to teach us to discern, to keep us from blindly accepting what appears to feed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He threw meal into the pot and said: Serve it—and the harm was gone. The simple thing made the poisoned clean. The Lord can sanctify what has been corrupted, if we invite His power into it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man from Baal Shalishah brought first fruits—twenty loaves and fresh ears of grain. He gave from the harvest itself, not from surplus. Such firstlings are a sign of trust that the Lord will provide the rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Give to the people, that they may eat; the Lord says they will eat and have leftovers—the prophet speaks abundance into scarcity. His faith isn't in the food but in the Lord's multiplication.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: we serve a God who multiplies small gifts into abundance, who restores what was lost, who lies down beside our dead, who turns poison to plenty. From the widow's jar to the Shunammite's son to the twenty loaves, the same God whispers: I am enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
